If you look up even a little bit of reference from Gmail or Microsoft Outlook, you can tell that the current prompt itself isn't sufficiently thought through from the user's perspective. The area the user asked to modify is the 'date' information area. But now, by adding attachment information to the date information area, two different kinds of information appear jumbled together, and I think readability actually got worse. Also, in the previous design, both 'the date and time the mail was sent' were right-aligned, so it was easy for the user to immediately understand the information at a glance, but in design A only 'Mar 14' is placed somewhere other than fully right-aligned at the far end, which means the user has to think one extra time — so it's hard to call this a good change.

In the existing design, the 'date/time area' was perceived simply as an area that provides information. But with the attachment icon and the words '1 file' added, I think users could get confused, like 'Does this take me somewhere if I click it?' I think this is a prompt that wasn't considered deeply enough from a UX perspective, and the designer should have looked at references from other services more thoroughly. If they had, they would have known it's more common to put attachments below the 'mail body' as chip buttons rather than in the 'date/time area', and I don't think they would have requested this change.
This is output generated from a prompt requested by a designer who hadn't thought deeply about UX, and since the input was low quality, I judged the output to be low quality as well.

And if other information absolutely has to be added, you shouldn't rely on the progress bar alone — you'd need to think harder about expressing it with a different kind of UI element.

1. Communities? Podcast? Unsuitable UX writing
When I first saw the existing mockup I perceived it as a community (social) screen, but seeing words like 'new releases' and 'quiet playlists' among the information representing each community made me wonder — does this mean podcasts rather than communities? It was confusing. The fact that the AI output failed to catch this unsuitability and just carried the data over as-is again raises doubts about AI's UXUI design expertise.

2. There seem to be many edits that simply generate plain 'text' rather than conveying information to the user through visual elements.
The 'very active' element is conveyed only as text in variant A, and with such a design it's hard for users to notice unless they read every bit of text carefully. Apart from long-term users, most users have only a certain amount of energy and time to spend, but this mockup forces the user to read each piece of information more than necessary. If this mockup were an actually released service, I'd expect a high churn rate among new users due to the inconvenient UX.
I didn't particularly find any unnecessary changes.

The brand color blue is used so much that it's overall cluttered and the content doesn't register at a glance. The recently updated Korail Plus (formerly Korail Talk) app has been getting a lot of criticism for updating only the visuals without any consideration for UX, and some reviews had negative reactions saying the updated design looked AI-made. And I felt this mockup also brings to mind Korail Plus's new UI. For example, if you look at the Korail Plus train schedule search list screen, you can see it uses many highly saturated colors (the badges indicating KTX, Mugunghwa, ITX, etc.) and a varied color palette — but in fact, in UXUI design you should strip away color as much as possible and apply accent colors only to important information. Most of the work GenUI has edited so far has the problem of indiscriminate use of the primary color and using more colors than necessary.
For the reasons mentioned in the readability comment above, I think the overall aesthetics and level of polish naturally became lower as well.

As a designer, assuming this mockup were the AI's output for the prompt I requested, I'd think this AI generates only a single fragmentary 'plausible-looking' screen without considering the UX flow at all. UXUI design isn't about drawing one screen — you have to consider many complex and varied UX flows — but based on the GenUI outputs so far, if you asked it to 'draw a sign-up screen' it seems it would generate only a shallow result without considering the various cases below. And I think this would negatively affect building trust in the service.

* Where does tapping 'log in' on that sign-up screen take you, does it go straight to the home screen or is an onboarding step needed, which SNS login options will be added for social account login and why, should those SNS login buttons be wide rectangular buttons or circular buttons to minimize space as much as possible, which wording is more appropriate among 'Get started / Continue / Log in', is it better to include the app service name on the login screen or not, which is more appropriate between email login and an in-house service account login design, etc.

The Promo code row label changed from 'Promo code / LISTEN10 applied' to 'Discounts / 2 offers applied'. It's a change outside the requested scope (the order summary card), but it's consistent in wording with the newly added discount breakdown and it tells you in advance that 2 benefits are applied, so it isn't disruptive. Still, it's a shame that its original character as the promo code entry/confirmation point is weakened.

The original summary was a flat 3-line structure, but now there's an added level: a subheading (Discount breakdown) + indented sub-items + a subtotal (Total discounts). The relationship between the top-level total and the detail items is clearer, so the hierarchy improved.

With the original 'Promo code' row changed to 'Discounts', the cue that this is where you enter or change a promo code is weakened. The value also changed from 'LISTEN10 applied' to '2 offers applied', so it's hard to tell which code is applied just from that row.

This version reflects the request accurately and with restraint. It breaks the single discount line into a member discount and the LISTEN10 promo and even shows a subtotal, so the original question — 'how much did I save with the promo code?' — is answered right away. It reuses the original typography and row styles, so there's almost no sense of inconsistency. The downsides are: (1) 4% = $2.34 but it's written as $2.35, so the rounding is off; (2) there's no on-screen basis for the 6%/4% split, so it looks arbitrary; (3) changing the 'Promo code' row to 'Discounts' weakens the cue for where to enter a code. All three are easy to fix at the copy level.

Placing a block that groups the individual benefits under the Discounts total makes the 'total - component items' relationship clear, and with a description line attached to each item the two-tier structure reads well. However, the header's 'You save $5.85' repeats the same value as the Discounts line, so the top-level information appears twice, which is hierarchical redundancy.

The discount items are grouped in a light background block, so they catch the eye first within the summary. The amounts and item names are similar in size to the original body text, so it's not hard to read. However, the description lines ('10% on albums and podcasts', etc.) are in gray lowercase, so contrast against the background is somewhat low.

A new nested structure was introduced with a card inside a card, and the summary got taller so the checkout button gets pushed down. On the other hand, the padding inside the block is tidy, so it doesn't feel cramped. Hard to call it better or worse.

With another orange-toned emphasis block added inside the card, the strongest color on the screen is now split between two places along with the checkout button. It looks closer to a promotional banner than the original's plain summary tone, and having 'You save $5.85' and 'Discounts -$5.85' state the same value twice also lowers the finish quality a bit.

It interpreted the request most faithfully, and above all the numbers match the cart contents exactly (10% of $32.97 for albums+podcasts = $3.30, 10% of $25.48 for video = $2.55, total $5.85). It even explains in one line what each benefit applies to, so the promo code's contribution is clearly visible, and it left the 'Promo code' row as is, so there are no changes outside the request. On the other hand, adding the orange emphasis block and the 'You save $5.85' badge splits attention with the checkout button, and the same amount is shown twice. If the emphasis were dialed back one notch (remove the badge or make the block neutral), it would look almost flawless.
